question: Hádanka: Moje meno sa od vášho líši len pár písmenami, aj ja mám bielo-modro-červenú vlajku so štítom a cudzinci si ma s vami pletú tak často, že ambasády si posielajú poštu, ktorá prišla na zlú adresu. Kto som?
source_excerpt: The flag of Slovenia consists of three equal horizontal bands of white, blue, and red, with the national coat of arms placed in the upper hoist side.

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks live this mix-up personally. The clues build playfully to an answer every Slovak knows, so the player feels clever and amused rather than tested.
extra.verification_notes: Slovenia's flag is white-blue-red with a coat-of-arms shield like Slovakia's, the names differ by a couple of letters, and no other country fits; no newer event affects this (checked from prior knowledge, no search run).

explanation: Slovensko a Slovinsko si zamieňajú novinári, športoví usporiadatelia aj prezidenti. George W. Bush si ich kedysi pomýlil v rozhovore.

question: Dokončite vetu: Keď vám Poliak v Zakopanom povie, že si odbehne do „sklepu“, nejde do pivnice, ale ide…
source_excerpt: establishment that sells goods or services to the public

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks often visit Poland, for example Zakopane, and assume 'sklep' means a cellar. The player can work it out from context: where does a Pole go every day?
extra.verification_notes: Polish 'sklep' means shop/store (cellar is only a rare, secondary sense), so 'do obchodu' is correct; source https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sklep

explanation: Po poľsky je „sklep“ obyčajný obchod. Podobne zradná je „uroda“, ktorá v poľštine neznamená úrodu, ale krásu.

question: Pravda alebo nepravda: Auto Chevrolet Nova sa v Latinskej Amerike nepredávalo, pretože „no va“ znamená po španielsky „nejde“.
source_excerpt: Third-generation Novas were assembled in Mexico City in 1973–1974, and fourth-generation Novas in 1975–1978.

extra.why_interesting: This is one of the most repeated 'translation blunder' stories in business textbooks, so players confidently say true. The twist is that the famous blunder is itself a blunder.
extra.verification_notes: The Nova was sold in Latin America (e.g., Mexico, Argentina), so the 'no va' claim is a myth and 'Nepravda' is correct; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Nova

explanation: Je to slávny mýtus z učebníc marketingu: Nova sa napríklad v Mexiku a vo Venezuele predávala slušne. Španiel by navyše „nova“ nečítal ako „no va“, rovnako ako my v slove „nová“ nepočujeme „no“.

question: Michelangelov Mojžiš má na hlave niečo, čo tam podľa pôvodnej Biblie nepatrí. Prekladateľ do latinčiny totiž namiesto „tvár mu žiarila“ napísal niečo celkom iné. Čo teda Mojžišovi vyrástlo na hlave?
source_excerpt: The Vulgate describes Moses' face in Exodus 34 as "cornuta" ("horned"), but the Hebrew original was difficult, and it probably didn't mean horns.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Moses as a solemn bearded prophet. They may half-remember something odd on the famous statue's head without ever knowing why. The stem gives the 'shining' clue, so the leap from rays of light to horns is a satisfying 'of course' moment. It also reveals that one translation choice shaped art for centuries.
extra.verification_notes: The Vulgate rendered Exodus 34 as 'cornuta' (horned), so Moses got horns; confirmed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_(Michelangelo).

explanation: Hebrejské slovo pre „žiariť“ je príbuzné so slovom „roh“, a tak svätý Hieronym v latinskej Biblii napísal, že Mojžišova tvár bola „rohatá“. Umelci potom Mojžiša celé stáročia poctivo zobrazovali s rohmi.
